text.text: Your estate planning practice in one place. Follow each Engagement through consultation, drafting, signing and funding, keep Instruments and Signings moving, and use Review due on Clients to bring past clients back. Operational tracking only; it holds no legal advice.
A smooth engagement takes six to ten weeks. The usual delay is the information-gathering stage, so make that step easy for clients.
Learn the family: spouse or partner, children (and whether any are minors or have special needs), blended family, who they trust.
Learn the assets roughly: home, accounts, retirement plans, life insurance, business interests, property in other states.
Recommend a package (will, revocable trust, plan update) and explain why in plain words.
Questionnaire sent with a return date two weeks out
Asset list with how each asset is titled and who the beneficiaries are
Copies of deeds and existing plans
Choices made: executor or trustee, guardians for minor children, agents under powers of attorney, healthcare agents, who inherits what
Call clients who have not returned the questionnaire after ten days. Offer to complete it with them on a call.
Add one instrument row per document. Draft from the firm's forms; never from a client's online template.
Attorney reviews every instrument before the client sees it.
Send drafts with a one-page summary in plain language. Hold a review meeting; changes go back to drafting.
) before or at signing, as your engagement letter says.
The Okoye trust is in drafting, the pour-over wills are three days late and the powers of attorney are due in 12 days. The paralegal finishes the wills this week so the signing in 18 days holds.

text.text: A will or trust signed without the right formalities may fail when it is needed. Signing day is run from a checklist every time.
Two witnesses booked who are not named in the documents (tick
Client told what to bring: photo ID, glasses, and any spouse who must sign
Room booked, or a home visit planned for clients who cannot travel
Attorney meets the clients first, alone if there is any question of influence, and confirms they understand and agree.
Walk through each document's purpose, briefly.
Sign in order: trust, wills, powers of attorney, directives, deeds. Witnesses and notary sign as each document requires.
Check every signature page before anyone leaves: dates, initials, witness addresses, notary seal.
Only where your state allows remote witnessing and notarization. Follow the state's process exactly and keep the recording if required.
Signed copies sent to the client with a summary letter
Funding steps created for every asset going into the trust

If a client seems confused, or a family member answers every question for them, the attorney stops and meets the client alone. Note what was asked and answered. A short delay is better than a plan that is challenged later.
If someone is ill or absent
Reschedule rather than sign without the formalities. Mark the signing
with the reason and book a new date.
The Fairbairns' first signing was moved when Winston was ill. The new signing is in two days; the trust and directives are ready and both witnesses and the notary are booked.
A revocable trust only avoids probate for assets it owns. An unfunded trust is the most common reason a carefully drafted plan fails. Funding is part of the job, not an afterthought.
For every asset on the client's asset list, add a funding step:

Call clients about anything past due. Offer to join a call with their bank.

, send a final letter listing what is in the trust, and remind the client that new assets must be titled in the trust too.

Leopold's checking account retitle is overdue; his brokerage retitle and life policy beneficiary change are due this week. The paralegal calls him today and offers a three-way call with the credit union.
Real estate in another state needs a deed recorded in that state, often by a local lawyer. Start it early; it is usually the slowest step.
Never retitle retirement accounts into the trust without the attorney's review.
Never mark a step done on the client's word alone.
Plans go stale: families change, laws change, assets change. Regular reviews keep plans working and bring steady, welcome work to the practice.
Every three to five years as a routine.
After a marriage, divorce, birth, death, move to another state, sale of a business, large inheritance or a child turning 18.

text.text: The Penhallows' plan was signed about five years ago and they have since moved states. Their review was due 30 days ago; the amendment engagement is in attorney review with a signing set for this week.

A plan signed in another state is usually still valid, but powers of attorney, healthcare directives and property rules differ by state. Treat any move as a reason for a full review, not a quick call.
Clients do not like to think about this. Keep reminders short, warm and free of pressure, and make booking easy.

Decide your answer before the first call: many practices offer the review call free and quote any amendment or new plan as a fixed fee. Write the fee on the engagement so the client knows the number before any drafting starts.

The production desk of an estate planning practice: each engagement from consultation to a funded trust, every instrument being drafted, signing appointments, the assets still to move into trusts, and clients due for a review. Drafts live in your document system.
